terms.definition: "Stand by what has been decided": courts follow the decisions of earlier cases on similar facts, and lower courts are bound by higher courts.
terms.examiner: It is what gives precedent its certainty and fairness; link it to the court hierarchy when a question asks how precedent operates.

terms.definition: The reason for the decision: the legal principle on which the judgment is based. It is the part of the judgment that binds later courts.
terms.examiner: Distinguish it from the facts and from obiter dicta. A judgment can have more than one ratio.

terms.definition: "Other things said": the rest of the judgment, including hypothetical situations. It does not bind but can be persuasive.
terms.examiner: Howe: the obiter statement that duress is no defence to attempted murder was followed in Gotts.

terms.definition: A decision of a higher court (or sometimes the same court) that a later court must follow where the material facts are sufficiently similar.
terms.examiner: Use the hierarchy: the Supreme Court binds all courts below it; the Court of Appeal is bound by the Supreme Court and generally by itself.

terms.definition: A precedent that a court is not bound to follow but may choose to.
terms.examiner: Sources: lower courts (R v R), the Privy Council (The Wagon Mound), obiter dicta (Howe), dissenting judgments, and courts of other countries.

terms.definition: The statement allowing the House of Lords, now the Supreme Court, to depart from its own previous decisions when it appears right to do so.
terms.examiner: Herrington v British Railways Board (departing from Addie v Dumbreck) in civil law; Shivpuri (overruling Anderton v Ryan) in criminal law. It is used sparingly.

terms.definition: The Court of Appeal is bound by its own decisions except where two of its decisions conflict, where a later Supreme Court or House of Lords decision has impliedly overruled its decision, or where the decision was made per incuriam.
terms.examiner: The Criminal Division has extra flexibility where the liberty of the subject is at stake (Taylor, Gould).

terms.definition: Overruling: a court in a later case states that the legal rule in an earlier case is wrong. Reversing: a higher court overturns the decision of a lower court in the same case on appeal. Distinguishing: a judge avoids a precedent because the material facts are different.
terms.examiner: Distinguishing: Balfour v Balfour and Merritt v Merritt. These are the tools that give precedent its flexibility.
